title: Blockbuster Could Have Bought Netflix for $50 Million

scenes.narration: In September 2000, three men from a small, money-losing startup flew to Dallas with an offer.
Buy us for fifty million dollars, they said, and we'll run your business online.
The startup was Netflix. The answer was no.

visual.text: The answer was no.
visual.subtitle: The startup was Netflix

scenes.narration: Everyone knows that part. What most people don't know is that Blockbuster fought back, and for a moment, it was winning.

visual.text: Blockbuster fought back. For a moment, it was winning.

scenes.narration: This is Built and Broken. Episode three. Blockbuster.

visual.text: BLOCKBUSTER
visual.subtitle: Built & Broken · Episode 3

scenes.narration: On the nineteenth of October 1985, a businessman named David Cook opened the first Blockbuster store in Dallas, Texas.

visual.subtitle: David Cook opens the first Blockbuster in Dallas

scenes.narration: Most video shops back then were small and cramped. Cook's store was big and bright, with around eight thousand tapes on the shelves and a computerized checkout.

visual.title: A new kind of video shop

scenes.narration: In 1987, an entrepreneur named Wayne Huizenga took control and did what he did best. He expanded. Fast.

visual.text: 1987: Wayne Huizenga takes control. Expand. Fast.

scenes.narration: Blockbuster spread across America and then the world. Friday night meant one thing. Walk the aisles, pick a movie, grab some popcorn at the counter.

visual.text: Friday night
visual.subtitle: Walk the aisles. Pick a movie. Popcorn at the counter.

scenes.narration: In 1994, the media giant Viacom bought Blockbuster in a deal worth eight point four billion dollars.
By 2004, Blockbuster was at its peak. More than nine thousand stores. Eighty four thousand employees. Six point one billion dollars in revenue in a single year.
scenes.note: 2004 10-K: 9,094 stores, about 84,300 employees, $6.1 billion revenue. Grid values are rounded because the KPI grid only animates whole numbers.

scenes.narration: But there was a secret inside that business, and every customer knew it. Late fees.

visual.text: Late fees.
visual.subtitle: The secret every customer knew

scenes.narration: Return a tape a day late, and you paid. In 2000, Blockbuster collected nearly eight hundred million dollars in late fees.
That was about sixteen percent of its revenue. One dollar in every six came from customers making a mistake.
Remember that number. A business that makes money when its customers are unhappy is a business waiting for a competitor.

visual.title: Remember this
visual.text: A business that profits when its customers are unhappy is waiting for a competitor.

scenes.narration: That competitor started in 1997. Netflix rented DVDs by mail, and, eventually, with no late fees at all.

visual.title: Two ways to rent a movie

scenes.narration: By 2000, the dot-com bubble had burst, and Netflix was losing money. So its founders, Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, with their finance chief Barry McCarthy, went to Dallas.

visual.text: Reed Hastings, Marc Randolph and Barry McCarthy fly to Dallas

scenes.narration: Their pitch: Netflix would become Blockbuster's online business. The price, fifty million dollars.

visual.title: The pitch
visual.text: Netflix becomes Blockbuster's online business. Price: $50 million.

scenes.narration: Marc Randolph later wrote that Blockbuster's chief executive, John Antioco, was struggling not to laugh.

visual.title: Marc Randolph, Netflix co-founder
visual.text: John Antioco was struggling not to laugh.

scenes.narration: McCarthy put it more bluntly. They laughed us out of their office.

visual.title: Barry McCarthy, 2008
visual.text: They laughed us out of their office.

scenes.narration: To be fair, it looked like a sensible decision at the time. Netflix was tiny and unprofitable. Blockbuster was making billions.
Netflix flew home and decided to beat them instead. By the end of 2006, it had six million subscribers.

visual.subtitle: Netflix subscribers by the end of 2006

scenes.narration: Here is the part that usually gets left out. Blockbuster did not ignore Netflix forever.

visual.text: Blockbuster did not ignore Netflix forever.

scenes.narration: In 2004 it launched Blockbuster Online. And on the first of January 2005, it did something remarkable. It scrapped late fees.
It was expensive. By one estimate, ending late fees cost about two hundred million dollars, and launching the online business cost about two hundred million more.

visual.title: Estimated cost of the fight back ($ millions)

scenes.narration: Then, in late 2006, Blockbuster played the one card Netflix could never match. Its stores.

visual.text: Its stores.
visual.subtitle: The one card Netflix could never match

scenes.narration: It was called Total Access. Rent a DVD online, and when you were done, you could return it to any Blockbuster store and walk out with another movie for free.

visual.title: Total Access, 2006
visual.text: Rent online. Return it in a store. Walk out with another movie, free.

scenes.narration: Customers loved it. Total Access passed two million subscribers, and inside Netflix, people were worried. Blockbuster was spending heavily, and it was working.
And then Blockbuster turned on itself.

visual.text: And then Blockbuster turned on itself.

scenes.narration: The fight with Netflix was costing money, and the company was in debt. The activist investor Carl Icahn, who held a large stake and sat on the board, questioned the spending.

visual.text: Debt. Heavy spending. An activist investor on the board: Carl Icahn.

scenes.narration: Antioco clashed with the board over his pay, and in 2007 he left.

visual.subtitle: John Antioco leaves after a fight with the board

scenes.narration: His replacement was Jim Keyes, the former boss of the convenience store chain Seven-Eleven. He believed the future was still in stores.
Money was running short. Marketing for the online service had already been cut back, and under Keyes, Total Access became more expensive. Subscriber growth stalled.

visual.text: Marketing cut back. Prices up. Growth stalled.

scenes.narration: Blockbuster had built a real answer to Netflix, and then it took its foot off the pedal.

visual.text: Foot off the pedal
visual.subtitle: Blockbuster stops pushing its own answer

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the ground was moving. In January 2007, Netflix launched streaming. Just a thousand films at first, but no disc, no envelope, no store.
And from the other side came Redbox. Red kiosks outside supermarkets, renting DVDs for a dollar a night. By 2008, Redbox had more locations in America than Blockbuster.
Blockbuster was squeezed between the convenience of streaming and the price of a vending machine. Its stores, once its greatest strength, were now a giant fixed cost.

visual.text: Its greatest strength became its biggest cost.

scenes.narration: On the twenty third of September 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy.
That same year, Netflix passed twenty million subscribers.

visual.subtitle: Netflix subscribers at the end of 2010

scenes.narration: In 2011, the satellite TV company Dish bought what was left of Blockbuster at auction for about three hundred and twenty million dollars. In 2014, Dish closed the last company-owned stores.
By 2019, there was just one Blockbuster left on Earth. An independently owned store in Bend, Oregon, that kept the name.

visual.text: One left.
visual.subtitle: Bend, Oregon

scenes.narration: Kodak protected its profits. Nokia measured the wrong thing.
Blockbuster's story is stranger. It found the right answer. It paid for it. It was winning. And then it stopped.

visual.text: It found the answer. It paid for it. It was winning. Then it stopped.

scenes.narration: Fighting a disruptor costs money, and the bill arrives long before the reward. Blockbuster blinked when the bill arrived.

visual.title: The lesson
visual.text: Fighting a disruptor costs money now. The reward comes later. Blockbuster blinked.

scenes.narration: Fifty million dollars was the cheapest chance it ever had. Every chance after that cost more, and it took fewer of them.

visual.subtitle: The cheapest chance Blockbuster ever had

scenes.narration: This has been Built and Broken. Subscribe for the next story of a giant that saw the future, and still fell.
